To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the first field measurements of brown carbon (BrCs) in the marine atmospheric aerosols have been made over the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea.

light absorbing organic aerosol (brown carbon) in the marine atmospheric layer (MABL), over the tropical Indian ocean is significantly influenced by the continental outflow, and the mass absorption efficiency (σabs) of brown carbon is comparable with that of elemental carbon.

brown carbon (BrCs) in the marine atmospheric layer of tropical Indian Ocean has a significant impact on the atmospheric radiative forcing, and this impact is mainly from the biomass burning emissions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the first field measurements of brown carbon in the MABL over the tropical Indian ocean and provides a better understanding of the radiative forcing of aerosols in this region.
the impact of biomass burning aerosols on the radiative forcing of the Earth’s climate.
a first field measurement of BrC and its radiative impact over a tropical Indian Ocean region.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the BrC is a significant component of the aerosol absorption in the MABL of the BoB and the ARS, and the mass absorption efficiency is similar to that observed in the continental air over the IGP.
the BrC in MABL over BoB and ARS is mainly due to biomass burning emissions.
the light absorbing water-solute organic carbon (brown carbon) is a significant contributor to the light absorption properties of aerosols over oceanic regions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

brown carbon is a significant component of light absorbing aerosols over oceanic regions and its contribution increases with the proximity of pollution source regions, which may be a significant factor in the radiative forcing of the Earth's climate.
the BrC in aerosols is an important contributor to the atmospheric absorption properties and the radiative forcing over the oceanic region.
the mass absorption efficiency and Angstrom exponent of brown carbon over the tropical Indian region are quite similar to those reported from other oceanic regions.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the brown carbon is a significant component of the total light absorption of the atmospheric aerosols over oceanic regions, and it needs to be taken into account in climate models to better understand the role of aerosol in the climate forcing.

the contribution of brown carbon to the absorption properties is significant over the oceanic regions located at a distance of ∼1000–2000 km from the pollution sources, and it needs to be considered for accurate assessment of aerosol radiative forcing.
the contribution of BrC to aerosol absorption is not limited to continental regions, but is also important over the oceans.
